name: PIQA: Physical Interaction Question Answering
description: PIQA is a benchmark dataset for evaluating physical commonsense reasoning in natural language understanding systems. The dataset consists of multiple choice question answering pairs where a model must choose the most appropriate solution to a physical goal. It contains over 16,000 training QA pairs with approximately 2K development and 3K test examples. The dataset is inspired by instructables.com and focuses on everyday situations with a preference for atypical solutions.
creator: Yonatan Bisk, Rowan Zellers, Ronan Le Bras, Jianfeng Gao, Yejin Choi
publisher: Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AAAI)
citeAs: Bisk, Y., Zellers, R., Le Bras, R., Gao, J., and Choi, Y. 2020. PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language. In AAAI.
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected using Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) annotators who were prompted with links to instructables.com. Annotators were asked to glance at instructions from an instructable and construct two component tasks, articulating a physical goal and how to achieve it, along with a subtle incorrect permutation (trick). Annotators were seeded with instructables from six categories: costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop. Two examples were drawn per instructable. A qualification HIT was run prior to the main annotation, and validation HITs were run afterwards. Data was collected in batches of several thousand triples and validated by other annotators for correctness.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed from the data. This often meant that correct examples were removed that required expert level knowledge of a domain (e.g., special woodworking terminology) which should not fall under the umbrella of commonsense.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Instructions and project descriptions from instructables.com, a crowdsourced collection of instructions for activities ranging from cooking to car repair. Annotators used these as inspiration to construct goal-solution pairs.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The AFLite algorithm was used to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples from the data. AFLite performs systematic data bias reduction by discarding instances whose feature representations are collectively highly indicative of the target label. 5,000 examples from the original dataset were used to fine-tune BERT-Large, and the corresponding embeddings of all remaining instances were computed. AFLite uses an ensemble of linear classifiers trained on random subsets of the data to determine whether pre-computed embeddings are strong indicators of the correct answer option.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Goals were tokenized by Spacy. The AFLite algorithm was applied to remove annotation artifacts and spurious biases. Train, development, and test folds were automatically produced by AFLite. Examples were truncated at 150 tokens for model experiments, affecting 1% of the data. A diff button was included in the annotation interface to highlight differences between solutions.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were provided with links to instructables.com as inspiration. They were asked to: (1) provide a physical goal, (2) provide a valid solution, and (3) provide a trick - a solution that sounds reasonable but is wrong, often due to a subtle misunderstanding of preconditions or physics. Additional HITs were run for qualification prior to the main annotation stage and for validation afterwards. Annotators had to successfully identify well-formed vs. underspecified goal-solution pairs with >80% accuracy to participate in the main HIT. Data was validated by other annotators for correctness. Users with low agreement were de-qualified.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Examples with low inter-annotator agreement during validation were removed from the dataset. Human performance was calculated by majority vote among annotators who achieved >=90% on the qualification HIT. Annotator pay averaged >$15/hr according to self-reporting on turkerview.com and timing calculations.
rai:annotationsPerItem: Multiple annotators per item for validation; human performance calculated by majority vote
rai:machineAnnotationTools: AFLite algorithm (using BERT-Large embeddings and ensemble of linear classifiers); Spacy for tokenization; GPT BPE tokenizer for sequence length analysis
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance physical commonsense reasoning in AI systems, which is relevant for building robots that interact with the world and understand natural language. The authors argue that knowledge should be learned from interaction with the world to eventually be communicated with language, and that language-only learning is limiting for physical understanding.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset was constructed to be adversarial to BERT. Reporting bias was identified as a challenge during data collection, where annotators tended toward prototypical solutions and common tools. AFLite was applied to reduce annotation artifacts. The dataset was specifically designed to flatten the distribution of referenced objects to counteract reporting bias.
rai:dataLimitations: Large pretrained models struggle with the dataset (~77% accuracy vs. 95% human accuracy). The dataset focuses on English only. Some correct examples requiring expert-level domain knowledge were removed during validation. Models trained on large web crawls may eventually surpass human performance, as some human 'mistakes' were actually correct answers requiring web search to verify. The dataset may not capture the full breadth of physical commonsense knowledge.
rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking and evaluation of physical commonsense reasoning in natural language understanding models. The dataset is intended for testing/evaluation purposes to measure the gap between model and human performance on physical commonsense tasks. It can also be used as a diagnostic tool to probe the physical knowledge encoded in pretrained language models.
